idiom_name: hand-written forwarder/receiver over POSIX sockets with a length-prefixed frame
implementation_notes: C has no messaging runtime, so both roles are ordinary translation units: the forwarder resolves the destination through a name-to-sockaddr table (getaddrinfo/socket/connect), serialises the message into a byte buffer with an explicit header in network byte order (a 32-bit length plus a small type tag) and hands the iovec list to writev()/send(); the receiver owns its own loop over recv()/poll(), reads the header first and then loops until the body is complete before dispatching through a table of peer function pointers. Nothing in the standard library replaces the classic structure, so the structure is the implementation; the only real leverage is to keep encode/decode in one place so a portable codec (protobuf-c, XDR) can replace the hand-written one, and to keep the socket calls behind the two roles so a second mechanism can be added.
pitfalls: send()/recv() on a stream socket return partial counts; every read and write must loop, and the length header must be read before the body is allocated.
Writing to a closed peer raises SIGPIPE and kills the process unless MSG_NOSIGNAL is set or the signal is ignored; the error still arrives as EPIPE.
Never memcpy a struct layout onto the wire: padding, alignment and endianness differ between peers - serialise field by field.
An unbounded length field is an allocation-based denial of service, and every byte the receiver validates is data from an untrusted source.
